title: The 10 million ceiling on Target Liquidity means instant-withdrawal coverage shrinks as a vault grows
content:
Target Liquidity is "the amount of deposited assets that should remain within each Spark Savings vault contract to support instant withdrawals" (A.6.1.1.1.3.5.3.1.1), and the live configuration is the same formula for all eight vaults: "the greater of 10% of total deposits or 1 million... **up to a maximum amount of 10 million**" (A.6.1.1.1.3.5.3.1.3.1 through .3.8; ETH uses 250 / 2,500 ETH).

The three terms bind in different regimes. Below 10 million in deposits, the 1 million floor dominates — a small vault holds a disproportionately large buffer. Between 10 and 100 million, the 10% term governs. **Above 100 million, the cap governs and the coverage ratio decays with every new deposit.**

That last regime is where the vaults actually live. The Ethereum USDT vault has a 4 billion supply cap and the USDC vault 2 billion; at full utilization, 10 million of instant liquidity is 0.25% and 0.5% respectively. The buffer sized for the vault's tenth depositor is the same buffer serving its ten-thousandth.

The cap is not obviously wrong — idle assets earn nothing, and the whole point of the Spark Liquidity Layer is to deploy deposits productively, so a literal 10% of 4 billion sitting still would be an enormous drag. But it means the instant-withdrawal promise is a promise about *typical* withdrawal sizes, not about the vault's ability to honour a run.

Everything else in this section exists because of that gap: the intents mechanism for larger redemptions, the relayer infrastructure that refills the buffer, and the Core Operator backstop when the relayer fails. The 10 million is a working float, and the Artifact is candid that the rest is a process, not a reserve.
description: Every vault holds the greater of 10% of deposits or 1 million, capped at 10 million — so past 100 million in deposits the percentage clause stops binding and the covered fraction falls.
